current_disclosures.section: Products, Market, and Sales > Product Technologies
current_disclosures.summary: DRAM products are volatile, low-latency memory devices used in various markets including data centers, PCs, and automotive. In 2025, the company began shipping the industry's first 1γ production node incorporating EUV lithography for improved efficiency, while the majority of DRAM bit production remained on the 1ß node. This portfolio includes specialized types such as High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM) for AI and high-performance computing, Double Data Rate (DDR) including DDR5, Low-Power DRAM (LPDDR) for mobile devices, and Graphics DRAM (GDDR) for graphics-intensive applications.

comparisons.peer_summary: The company provides advanced technology and IP platforms for customers to design ASICs targeting AI, high-performance computing, and networking applications.
comparisons.comparison: Both MU and AVGO identify 'high-performance computing' and 'AI' as primary target applications for their technologies. MU defines its HBM product as ideal for 'AI applications and high-performance computing'. AVGO states that its Custom Silicon Solutions (ASICs) target 'AI and high-performance computing, networking and storage applications'. While MU provides a specific memory architecture (HBM) to support these workloads, AVGO provides custom silicon platforms/ASICs for customers to design chips for these same workloads. The shared topic is the strategic focus on serving the AI and HPC market segments through specialized hardware.

sentences.text: This makes it ideal for applications that require high data throughput and energy efficiency, such as AI applications and high-performance computing.

• Custom Silicon Solutions: We provide advanced technology and intellectual property ("IP") platforms for customers to design and develop application specific integrated circuits ("ASICs") targeting AI and high-performance computing, networking and storage applications. Our custom silicon provides the platform to integrate embedded logic, memory, serializer/deserializer ("SerDes") technology, IP cores and processor cores. ASICs are custom products built to individual customers specifications.

peer_results.rationale: INTC candidates describe discrete client GPUs (Arc B-Series) and edge computing processors (Core Ultra). These focus on client graphics and edge CPUs rather than the high-bandwidth memory (HBM) architecture and data center/AI memory solutions described by MU.

comparisons.peer_summary: NVIDIA's key strategy involves advancing its accelerated computing platform to solve complex problems with higher performance and lower power consumption than alternatives. This full-stack innovation approach leverages GPUs, CUDA, and networking technologies to serve diverse end markets including Data Center, Gaming, Professional Visualization, and Automotive.
comparisons.comparison: Both MU and NVDA highlight that their respective product architectures are specifically optimized for AI and high-performance computing workloads, emphasizing a dual benefit of higher performance and lower power consumption. MU describes HBM as a '3D stacked DRAM architecture' that achieves 'higher bandwidth while consuming less power compared to other memory types' for AI applications. NVDA describes its 'accelerated computing platform' as capable of solving complex problems in 'significantly less time and with lower power consumption than alternative computational approaches', leveraging GPUs and networking for AI and data center markets. While MU focuses on the memory subsystem (HBM) enabling these gains, NVDA focuses on the processing platform (GPU/accelerator), both identify energy efficiency and AI suitability as core product value propositions.

sentences.text: High-Bandwidth Memory ("HBM"): A 3D stacked DRAM architecture that utilizes through-silicon via ("TSV") connections for a more efficient communication between each stack giving it the ability to achieve a higher bandwidth while consuming less power compared to other memory types.
This makes it ideal for applications that require high data throughput and energy efficiency, such as AI applications and high-performance computing.
Our accelerated computing platform can solve complex problems in significantly less time and with lower power consumption than alternative computational approaches.

While the computing requirements of these end markets are diverse, we address them with a unified underlying architecture leveraging our GPUs, CUDA and networking technologies as the fundamental building blocks.

comparisons.peer_topic: Product energy efficiency and Green500 performance
comparisons.peer_summary: NVIDIA's GPU-accelerated computing is optimized for energy efficiency and performance per watt, evidenced by NVIDIA powering 24 of the top 30 most energy-efficient systems, including the top supercomputer, on the Green500 list.
comparisons.comparison: Both disclosures emphasize energy efficiency as a key competitive advantage in the context of AI and high-performance computing. MU states that HBM consumes 'less power compared to other memory types', making it 'ideal for applications that require ... energy efficiency'. NVDA notes that 'GPU-accelerated computing is inherently more energy efficient than traditional computing' and highlights its dominance on the Green500 list, powering 24 of the top 30 most energy-efficient systems. Although MU refers to a specific memory component's efficiency and NVDA refers to system-level GPU efficiency, both use energy efficiency to justify their products' suitability for demanding AI/HPC workloads.

sentences.text: High-Bandwidth Memory ("HBM"): A 3D stacked DRAM architecture that utilizes through-silicon via ("TSV") connections for a more efficient communication between each stack giving it the ability to achieve a higher bandwidth while consuming less power compared to other memory types.
GPU-accelerated computing is inherently more energy efficient than traditional computing for many workloads because it is optimized for throughput, performance per watt, and certain AI workloads.
We powered 24 of the top 30 most energy efficient systems, including the top supercomputer, on the Green500 list.
